title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
formal: Do disjoint languages \(A,B\in \mathrm{NP}\) exist such that, for every disjoint pair \(C,D\in \mathrm{NP}\), there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with \(f(C)\subseteq A\) and \(f(D)\subseteq B\)?
definitions: All four languages consist of finite binary strings. NP means membership has a polynomial-length certificate checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Disjoint means \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(C\cap D=\varnothing\). The total function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* may depend on \((C,D)\); its running-time polynomial need not be universal across pairs. No requirement is imposed on \(f(x)\) when \(x\notin C\cup D\). Completeness uses one function for both sides, not two unrelated reductions.

context_blocks.text: A disjoint NP pair expresses two efficiently certifiable cases that cannot occur together. Complete pairs would provide a universal object for this kind of promise complexity.

Canonical disjoint pairs arise from propositional proof systems, tying the question to proof simulation and finite incompleteness. The existence of a p-optimal proof system would imply a complete pair, but the converse is not asserted. This card asks the pair-completeness question itself.

why: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
